newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Asian aliens rush to escape Bahrain crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Asian aliens rush to escape Bahrain crackdown.

text.p: Illegal aliens mainly from the Indian subcontinent are rushing to their embassies in Bahrain for help to avoid deportation under a threatened government crackdown, embassy officials said on Wednesday.
A Bahrain government official warned foreign workers staying in the island illegally to send their children home or face deportation.
"Since these children (have) been conceived outside the law, they are without legal status in Bahrain," Nasser al-Thawadi told daily Bahrain Tribune.
"These families will be assisted by the immigration authorities to clear their situation and legally leave the country."

Bahrain, a small island state which serves as the Gulf's banking and finance centre, last month gave foreign workers staying illegally a three-month amnesty until October 31 to legalise their status, leave the country or face penalties.
"We are very grateful to the government for the amnesty," a Bangladesh embassy spokesman said.
"We are expecting around 3,000 Bangladeshis who are staying illegally in Bahrain to turn up," he told Reuters.
He said embassy staff were working day and night to meet the deadline. "So far, 1,094 have turned up for help."
An Indian embassy spokesman estimated there were around 5,000 people staying illegally in the island.
"Around 1,700 people have taken application forms for issuing emergency certificates with one-way travel outpass," the spokesman told Reuters.
He said there were around 100,000 Indians living in Bahrain.

"We would like to make an appeal to all Indian nationals who do not hold valid residence permits or travel documents to come forward and make the most of this opportunity," an Indian embassy official said in remarks published this week.
"The proportion of Pakistani illegal stayers is very small," a Pakistani embassy spokesman said, adding they worked both in the public and the private sectors.
"In 1995 when the government announced an amnesty, around 379 Pakistanis took advantage. We expected between 300-350 people this time," he said. "So far around 85 came forward."
Members of Bahrain's Asian community including Bangladeshis and Indians have been victims of arson attacks in a sporadic wave of anti-government unrest which erupted in December 1994.
Some Bahrainis believe that foreign workers are taking away their jobs.
Bahrain's population grew by 3.6 percent in the year to the end of June to 620,378 from 598,625 mainly due to an increase in the number of foreigners, according to official figures.
Data from the Central Statistic Organisation (CSO) showed foreigners -- mainly from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the Philippines -- make up almost 39 percent of the population.
The number of foreigners in Bahrain grew by 4.8 percent to 240,423 in the year to June 30, 1997 and the number of nationals increased 2.9 percent to 379,955, CSO data showed.
